author: timneutkens
text:
**Update:** This has been released. See [the docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/basic-features/data-fetching#incremental-static-regeneration) for more information. The RFC will remain for historical context.

## Summary

Fully automatic re-rendering of statically exported pages without a full rebuild.

With regards to static site generators this feature has been referred to in multiple ways, most commonly "Incremental builds" or "Incremental rebuilds".

This RFC exclusively discusses API additions. All new functionality is completely backwards compatible and can be incrementally adopted. This RFC introduces no deprecations.

## Background

Next.js recently introduced support for [next-gen Static Generation](https://nextjs.org/docs/basic-features/pages) (SSG) in v9.3.

Generating static pages in Next.js using `getStaticProps` and `getStaticPaths` provides numerous upsides:

- **Faster Websites:** Generated files can be served from a global CDN close to your users
- **Reduced Costs:** Request are not rendered on-demand for every user

However static generation as it exists today has one downside that makes it hard to adopt for larger websites or applications:

Every time something changes in the database a full rebuild is required in order to see the change in one single page.

An example to illustrate this is when you make a change to a blogpost in a headless CMS, you could be only updating the title of one blog item. After you make the change the application would require a full rebuild of all pages, just to make that one change visible.

In order to make static sites scale we have to regenerate pages without needing a full build of the application.

What if we could generate a new version of the page on-demand when a new request comes in, but without having the user wait for the re-rendering?

Effectively re-rendering the page in the background while the previous version of the page keeps being served.

The background re-rendering could be triggered based on a timeout, similar to the way that `Cache-Control`'s `maxage` works, when the timeout is exceeded a background re-render is triggered when a request comes in.

This would look something like:

- The page defines what timeout is reasonable, this could be as low as 1 second
- When a new request comes in the statically generated page is served
- When a new request comes in and the defined timeout is exceeded:
  - The statically generated page is served
  - Next.js generates a new version of the page in the background and updates the static file for future requests
- When a new request comes in the updated static file is served

This model is pretty ideal for static generation:

- Works in the background, users always get a static response
- Pages get statically re-generated, including all changes from the CMS
- It's fully automatic, no need to trigger a full rebuild

This allows for true incremental rendering of static pages in Next.js.

After this RFC for incremental static generation is implemented we can extend it to do force revalidation, which would be useful for CMS providers that want to get the content updated as quickly as possible.

## Implementation

Next.js 9.3 introduced `getStaticProps`, in `getStaticProps` you'll be able to return a `revalidate` property in order to opt-in to automatically generating in the background when a request comes in:

```js
// pages/blog/[slug].js
export async function getStaticProps({ params }) {
  const post = await getBlogPostBySlug(params.slug);
  return {
    // Set the timeout for generating to 1 second
    // This timeout could be longer depending on how often data changes
    revalidate: 1,
    props: {
      post,
    },
  };
}
```

Keep in mind that the timeout defined is a timeout for when an incoming request will re-render in the background. Meaning that the first request after the timeout period will serve the previously rendered page and then the page is regenerated in the background.

When you opt-in to `revalidate` you get:

- Fully static rendering
- Automatic re-generation in the background when a request comes in

Co-authored with @rauchg @Timer
Special thanks to @juancampa @dav-is

1. We run **at most one** invalidation concurrently, and the call itself is usually super cheap. Consider that most headless CMS providers put your content in a CDN already **optimized for high read throughput**, so requests are incredibly cheap.

author: borekb
text:
Great to see another RFC in this area. A few specific points of feedback:

1: It took me a while to realize that this would happen on the server (or a serverless platform like Now) **at runtime**. The word _static_ is commonly associated with a build-time process, producing something that can be uploaded to a "dumb" CDN.

I sort of realize now that you're talking about the end user experience – they would always get a static HTML – but this RFC basically proposes a behavior that's similar to SSR + nginx microcache (please correct me if I'm wrong) and that's not commonly referred to as SSG.

2: With these micro-caching strategies, it's often problematic to set the "right" timeout. In fact, there often isn't _any_ one value. That's why most CMS's don't send aggressive `cache-control` headers and prefer to feel "slow" rather than outdated. I guess it's also why the example uses 1 second 😄.

You could argue that if you know your site, you can set this number sensibly but in my experience, it's always a tough choice.

3: In the RFC, it might be worth pointing out what this background re-rendering means for the backend uptime guarantees. With SSG, I can turn the headless CMS off after I've generated the site; here, I don't.

I assume that if the response from the backend is an error, the previously rendered HTML is still returned. This could also lead to situations where `/post/my-blog-post` already has the new title but `/category/my-category/page/2` still displays the old value (backend was unreliable; I used a different timeout for that page, etc.)

author: rauchg
text:
1. It's **incremental** static generation because the goal is to route directly from the edge to a **static file**, no server in between. This maximizes availability and performance.

2. Sending `cache-control` is a bad idea primarily because you'd cache on the end user's device, and users are unlikely to consume the content more than once, so it's a pointless optimization. Plus, at that point invalidation is impossible until time passes.

    I disagree that slow or unavailable is better than slightly behind. This feature exists primarily for the category of pages where that is the absolute correct tradeoff (in other words, this is a good fit for **eventual consistency**). Any page where the [amazon 100ms](https://www.gigaspaces.com/blog/amazon-found-every-100ms-of-latency-cost-them-1-in-sales/) rule applies: landing pages, marketing content, blog posts, e-commerce, travel, etc.

3. **You absolutely can turn off the backend and CMS**. You won't get **forward** updates, but all the HTML that you produced with `getStaticProps` and `getStaticPages` at build time will stay there.

text:
Adding my 2¢:

Regarding point (1), this is different than SSR + nginx microcache and opens up a wealth of possibilities in the future.

- Because this is SSG and not SSR, the first user-request will not be blocking and cannot 500 if your upstream CMS/etc is down. It's served **immediately from the file system** (or CDN edge when configured).
- Since this is a framework concern, we can declaratively express dependences between groups of pages that need to be invalidated. We have intent to explore returning a set of [keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrogate_key) from `getStaticProps` that would allow you to express a dependency graph (across pages) for an all-or-nothing incremental update.

Regarding point (2):

Revalidation on an interval is just the beginning for this feature! Using the same [keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrogate_key) mentioned above, we could allow you to trigger revalidations on-demand using an API endpoint.
This would change the model to be event-driven instead of interval-based.

Regarding point (3):

> With SSG, I can turn the headless CMS off after I've generated the site; here, I don't.

You can definitely turn off the upstream CMS, database, or API! This **is SSG**—your site will remain online and would return the latest incrementally generated content (or build-time content if the outage occurred between build and deploy).

Is there a way we can make this more clear in the RFC? Can you explain what made you think this may act like or be SSR?

author: Timer
text:
1. Revalidation is performing an incremental rebuild (akin to `next build`) and storing the result **on disk**. If you were to reboot your Next.js server after a few hours, the first request would be the last incremental rebuild! Similarly, user requests are always served from disk (or memory, with the disk being watched for changes)!

2. iSSG satisfies this use case perfectly! If you have 10,000+ product pages but only want to render your most popular 100 at build time, you can opt-into [the `fallback` behavior](https://nextjs.org/docs/basic-features/data-fetching#the-fallback-key-required) which allows static generation to be deferred until the first request.
When a user request comes in for a page not generated at build-time, they'll be served a static skeleton (the request will not block). You can then show a loading state on the client-side while the incremental build is happening specific for that page!

author: Timer
text:
3. Ah, good suggestion! For some initial clarity: Incremental Static Site Generation (iSSG) is a Next.js feature, versus Serverless Pre-Rendering (SPR) which is a [ZEIT Now Smart CDN](https://zeit.co/smart-cdn) feature.

The difference between these two approaches can be tersely summarized as such:

iSSG: First and foremost, this is real Static Site Generation via Next.js. No tricks!
User requests are **always served from disk**, and are never blocking or slow (similarly, always a `HIT` [served from cache] on ZEIT Now—there's never a cache miss). This means your website retains availability even if the upstream CMS/API/Database is unavailable.
Furthermore, iSSG is agnostic to your hosting infrastructure, and can be configured to work on any platform (no config necessary with `next start`). It is fully open source.

SPR: Serverless Pre-Rendering is a [Smart CDN](https://zeit.co/smart-cdn) feature which is agnostic to what framework you deploy with. This technology adapts frameworks which are server-rendered to act more like a static site, but can still suffer from some availability issues. Since the website isn't truly SSG, you may incur an outage if your upstream API is unavailable at the time of deploy or cache purge. iSSG is designed to solve these problems.

author: Timer
text:
@kevinwolfdev @fabb it is best practice to always run a proxy in front of Next.js when self hosting (for example, Nginx).

Nginx, when self hosting, is normally responsible for Gzipping responses from `next start` instance(s) and caching static assets in memory (`/_next/static`).

With the introduction of iSSG, you'd now want to configure your reverse proxy to cache your iSSG-powered pages by respecting the headers returned by `next start` (iSSG pages have `s-maxage` in their response). This cache would be shared across all of your reverse proxy (Nginx) instances, thus fixing the "divergence" of incremental rebuilds across instances. You'd want to have upstream-affinity keyed on the request path and load balanced appropriately (if not using a shared volume for the dist directory).

To deal with upstream failover, you could either tolerate the potentially stale read, or setup your `next start` instances to share a writable volume so they all read from the same copies.

Solving all of this complexity is what ZEIT Now is designed to do for you! But we respect the fact that you may want to self-host this.

----

Note: the quick and dirty way to get this working when self-hosting without any reverse proxies with shared caches would be to share the disk volume of all your Next.js server instances (K8S makes this easy). We don't suggest a proxyless-setup though, even without iSSG.

author: borekb
text:
@rauchg @Timer Thanks for your replies.

---

> Is there a way we can make this more clear in the RFC? Can you explain what made you think this may act like or be SSR?

I'm still trying to wrap my head around it 😄. SSG, so far _for me_, was always something like Jekyll, GitHub Pages, Gatsby or `next export`, i.e., I run a command on my computer (or CI), it produces a folder with a bunch of HTML and JS files in it, I upload it to a CDN (_any_ CDN, which is an important point) and that's it. This RFC requires a smart target environment, like a custom Node.js server running `next start` or ZEIT Now, and that's not how I typically think about SSG.

When I mentioned SSR, I specifically meant that the result is similar to **nginx microcache + SSR**. It shares some important traits with it I think:

- There needs to be something smart running on the server / target deployment infrastructure.
- Maybe except ZEIT Now, clients will be usually talking to the origin, not the edge.
- There are similar tradeoffs when setting microcache's period or Next.js' `revalidate`.
- The backend / CMS will see the same load in both scenarios.

I also agree that having this feature in the framework is beneficial, for reasons you mentioned or simply for people who don't run a proxy in front of their Next.js deployments. But in many ways, I still find it quite similar to SSR + cache, or do you find it grossly unfair?

---

> Because this is SSG and not SSR, the first user-request will not be blocking and cannot 500 if your upstream CMS/etc is down.

In our case (a large e-commerce site), the probability that a route is already SSG'd is relatively low – I think we would pre-render something like hundreds of routes out of the total of many tens of thousands, the rest would be `fallback: true`.

BTW, we're not yet sure if we'd be able to use this at all. As I understand it, `fallback: true` means that Googlebot, if it's the first visitor to a site, will get just "Loading...", not the real contents, which is a concern.

We also have some pure programming questions around this, for example, how do we propagate all data needs from all React components under the page component to the page component itself, but that's for another time.

---

> Revalidation on an interval is just the beginning for this feature! Using the same keys mentioned above, we could allow you to trigger revalidations on-demand using an API endpoint. This would change the model to be event-driven instead of interval-based.

That's actually one of the most exciting parts of this RFC, or its future evolutions. (Cache) invalidation is a tough problem, and always be, but at least you'll be trying to solve it in a single framework, not across various different technologies.

That's awesome and I'm really rooting for you guys here 🤞.

---

> You can definitely turn off the upstream CMS, database, or API!

That's an important point, thanks. You indeed can in some cases. I was thinking in terms of our use case, where we cannot afford to SSG the entire site ahead of time.

If the serverless nextjs implementation catches up on these features, that might also give an added value here of having things under one hood if using something like Cloudfront together with Lambdas.

We are updating the title of this RFC to "Incremental Static **Regeneration**", because Next.js already has technically shipped incremental *generation* for appending new pages after you've shipped to prod (as seen in this demo: https://static-tweet.now.sh/)

We wanted to be clear that this RFC primarily discussing ***updating existing pages***, by ***regenerating*** the HTML after the data has changed.

In general, we will continue to use the umbrella term "Incremental Static Generation" to refer to all the capabilities Next.js has for updating static content after you have already built your site, but we wanted to be extra clear for the context of this technical discusion.

"Incremental Static Generation" generally will refer to:
- Adding or removing pages (example: https://static-tweet.now.sh/)
- Preview mode (example: https://next-preview.now.sh/)
- Updating pages in the background (like this RFC discusses)
- Updating pages and _sets of pages_ eagerly when e.g.: CMS data changes (coming soon!)

author: timneutkens
text:
The problem with this reasoning is that it's not exactly stale-while-revalidate but an extra layer on top of it, e.g. generally you have maxage, s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate as a directive. Then s-maxage directs if a response should be cached after the first render. However with static generation the semantics are not the same, the html is generated at build time and then served before re-rendering in the background happens similar to stale-while-revalidate. Hence the name being just "revalidate" to not confuse the behavior, Next.js then handles the behavior for you (including setting the right headers).

We're planning to allow a bypass for bots though, so that they can always read the latest content. However this might also make the results worse given that the time to first byte will be significantly higher.

text:
Cache directives only deal with how to define the stale / freshness of a file / request. They have nothing to do with how it's rendered but could have something to do with when to fetch a fresh version. 

If you look at this feature like a cache then it'll be simplified and more familiar to developers using a battle-tested spec instead of creating a new "Nextjs spec" that combines several existing cache directives and creates cases where you need to create one-off solutions (like a bypass for bots). Who knows what the next one-off feature request will be? 

Caching is already used by most websites without bot exceptions (and many will put a cache in front of this service - invalidating the bot exception). Creating exceptions for bots is generally a bad idea (they should be crawling the same site that users see). 

Overall, I think as a maintainer you'd want to consider treating this like a cache, it might be slightly harder to implement up front but will save you down the road from all the edge cases and you'll always be able to reference the cache spec when answering questions. Not to mention the developers will get more control.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cache-Control

```
**max-age=<seconds>**
The maximum amount of time a resource is considered fresh. Unlike Expires, this directive is relative to the time of the request.

**s-maxage=<seconds>**
Overrides max-age or the Expires header, but only for shared caches (e.g., proxies). Ignored by private caches.

**stale-while-revalidate=<seconds>** 
Indicates the client will accept a stale response, while asynchronously checking in the background for a fresh one. The seconds value indicates how long the client will accept a stale response. See "Keeping things fresh with stale-while-revalidate" for more information.
```

author: janus-reith
text:
@CrocoDillon I was arguing about your reasoning for this:
> SSG it's probably for pages that don't change often

When you said: 
> So serving up to 1440 fallbacks per day

What I was pointing out is, that with just SSR you would have more pages to be rendered on-demand for that same scenario than the up to 1.440 falbacks you might have with revalidation, and therefore I don't consider that a valid reason to not use static generation. That's also where the sentence you quoted me regarding requests in between belongs, and I feel like you put it a bit out of context this way.
At the same time I pointed out that there certainly still is room for improvement how revalidation is trigggered, to have even less than those 1.440 renders of the page and still have up to date data. That's why I wrote two separate answers, one to @aej11a and one to you.

Regarding the general scenario, same for the weather app and the ecommerce sceanario that was brought up, I don't see how you consider up-to-date information critical, while at the same time not trying to solve that with client-side fetching.
Let's assume we don't use static generation and each time a viewer requests a product page it is rendered on demand - The viewer might get the current price at the time of rendering, but how does that make a difference?
The price could be changed a few seconds after the page was requested, and the viewer would still have a different price when adding to cart. The probability increases the longer that viewer keeps the page open.

I think I get the general point here, each time a user requests a page it should have the latest information to that point, and not an already outdated price, description.
However, a real way to solve this would be to have a way to programmatically trigger revalidation from your data source when necessary.
This might be more beneficial for the ecommerce scenario than the weather app, as there we might actually have an external data source in control, while that might not be a comparable case for the weather app.

In the meantime, getting the static page with another fetch for fresh data clientside still seems to be a more performant solution than doing SSR on demand each time, while this approach also has other benefits as it allows for actually up to date data, e.g. through polling. This can be optimized further by sending a hash or a db timestamp alongside the static props, so you could only compare that on a clientside fetch and fetch the product/weather data only when they differ.
Even if there already was a programmatical approach yet I guess this solution would still make more sense for the weather app, as there might be an near-infinite amount of new requested locations you don't want to rerender in the background each time.

The approch which was outlined here initially, where you do static generation but want a fallback loading show for users each x seconds again(could be more than one, e.g. 100 users could request the same not-yet-finished fallback page at the same time) IMHO seems to be a bit inconsistent on priorities.
That said, as mentioned before I agree that there might be some actual resonable cases where you want to do the data fetching only server-side inside `getStaticProps` and have a static page and don't want any viewers to possibly get the outdated version, I just can't really see them yet.

I see one point here that got me thinking: I aggree that there might be a bit additional effort to have your data available both to be fetchable clientside, and in `getStaticProps` - I wonder if some generalized method could be reasonable to be a able to trigger the same fetching done in `getStaticProps` again from the client as some endpoint where it will execute again to return the latest data. (Fetching an /api Route inside `getStaticProps` and reusing that is not.) But then again,`getStaticProps` might be handling many more data fetching from multiple endpoints for that page than what is relevant for the current information you are trying to get on the client, and selectively fetching from that `getStaticProps` API would make the whole construct more complex, so that might be hard to generalize.

author: lauroaraujo
text:
I tend to agree with @stevez86 , in the sense that we would definitely benefit from limiting the the time the stale cache can be valid.

I understand that it doesn't feel right to talk about limiting the time-to-live of a static page, but since we already have the `fallback` property that allows us to generate a static page on demand, I think it makes perfect sense to call the `fallback` if the content is "too stale".

A real world scenario for this is:
- I'm using `fallback` to generate product pages on demand.
- I've deployed today, (day 1)
- `user 1` visits the product page for a not-in-demand product and it gets cached.
- Tomorrow (day 2), something changes (price is the most common)
- A few days later (let's say day 5) `user 2` visits the page and gets the wrong data.

For that to happen, we need to not have deployed anything during this time, which is not too uncommon after a website is stable.

The reasoning to not want to re-generate the page after the content is "too stale" seems to be that it would be slow.

However, if I'm relying on `fallback` for that particular not-in-demand product, even if I rebuild the project, the first user to visit it will still have to wait for the page to be generated, so it's all the same.

I propose we are able to define **how long** the content can be stale, and if it's over that time, we use the `fallback` mechanism, just as if we had never generated that page at all.

Re-generating a page with other mechanisms (like hooks) is great to have, but may be overkill when just setting an expiry time would work.

author: timneutkens
text:
So the default with `next start` is a lru-cache based approach similar to https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/ssr-caching but built into Next.js in a way that works with the `stale-while-revalidate` semantics.

It also writes to disk by default currently: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/next-server/server/spr-cache.ts#L180. There's an experimental option to disable writing to disk `experimental: {sprFlushToDisk: false}` (name will likely change).

Next.js also sets the caching headers (`Cache-Control: s-maxage=<revalidate-time>, stale-while-revalidate`) so if you have a CDN in front of your application that supports caching dynamic responses it is handled automatically at the edge: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/next-server/server/send-payload.ts#L40. The writing to disk is in no way required if you have a CDN that supports caching dynamic responses.

In case of Vercel the revalidation is handled at the edge in a similar way to the Cache-Control approach described above.

> My suggestion is allowing a plugable cache, so deployments backed by ephemeral compute (like Firebase or AWS Serverlesss) can cache using blob storage (GCS/S3).

The main problem with this approach is that it's generally better to then invest resources into putting a CDN in front of your application given that then you don't have to go through functions in order to serve the static file. I'm not opposed to having a pluggable disk cache solution though, we'd just need to ensure it has the right characteristics for it to be as fast as possible.

author: timneutkens
text:
Posted a reply here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/11552#discussioncomment-22369

The TLDR of the post is:
Yes you need background compute, but it works with any CDN provider that supports `s-maxage` and `stale-while-revalidate` and does not require flushing to disk per-se. However the feature was built with having multiple ways to "revalidate" in mind so in the future it could potentially be expanded with a cli command to revalidate certain pages. We're starting with a programmatic way to do revalidation first though.

author: ceolinwill
text:
After using `unstable_revalidate` for a couple of weeks, there are two considerations I'd like to make which are preventing me from using SSG on all pages in my apps:

**1. SSR fallback**
A lack of an SSR fallback for SEO/SMO purposes as other people mentioned here and in [other threads](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/11646#issuecomment-640046701).

**2. Client-side regeneration**
`unstable_revalidate` doesn't seem to be called during client-side navigation. I'm not sure if that's a bug or a feature but that's a problem for my use case, where:

- The user visits a `post` page (e.g. `posts/123`);
- They visit the `edit` page (e.g. `posts/123/edit`), change something, and save their changes;
- They navigate back to the `post` page.

When they do so, the `post` page isn't revalidating the data. This means the same user would need to perform a force refresh (Cmd + R) twice to see their changes.

I'd expect the data to be regenerated once they visited the page again using client-side navigation. So, when they would refresh the page for the first time, the page would contain their changes.

**Considerations**

- Problem **1** could be solved if a `ssrFallback` option would be available or we could have the blocking-render option mentioned by @Timer.
- Problem **2** could be solved by regenerating the page when a user performs client-side navigation or when we have an API for event-driven regeneration, also mentioned that it's already on your plans.

Having those two features, I'd probably use SSG for most (or all) of pages on my Next.js apps. Great work!

author: ivawzh
text:
I am thinking in a case of using a cluster of servers and without a shared volume. Each server will keep its own copy of static props. When the cluster is large, there will be a risk that CDN unluckily always hit another server that revalidation frequency is met but the page is not yet rerendered. Such that, CDN will be serving dated contents for an unexpectedly long time.

One workaround I can think of to reduce the risk is to set the response header `Cache-Control` TTL to something shorter than revalidation frequency. E.g. `max-age=100` at header, and `{ revalidate: 200 }` on `getStaticProps`. That implies we need flexibility in controlling `getStaticProps`'s response header. 

Are there better ways to do it? 🤔

author: lukebarton
text:
Yes, this is a great point. This the problem with caching on each instance (application layer caching). Incidentally it's not a problem if you have precisely one instance.

What's jumping out at me is that static rendering and this revalidation feature are kind of redundant if you have a real cache proxy/CDN and just use cache headers correctly, using server side rendered content. Because if Next always renders server side, and you use `stale-while-revalidate`, then your CDN is going to behave exactly like Next tries to with `revalidate`, and lets you run a cluster of Next servers without worrying about what it's serving from the application cache.

It seems like Next is trying to give users an ad-hoc cache embedded into the application. I definitely think if Next wants to do that, it'd be better designed as a layer _around_ Next and activated via normal cache headers. Continuing down the current route as it stands kinda concerns me for reasons that Ivan points out, as well as a general concern for the coherence of Next itself.

author: timneutkens
text:
> What's jumping out at me is that static rendering and this revalidation feature are kind of redundant if you have a real cache proxy/CDN and just use cache headers correctly,

`stale-while-revalidate` is not supported if you don't have an enterprise plan on most CDN providers.

> It seems like Next is trying to give users an ad-hoc cache embedded into the application. I definitely think if Next wants to do that, it'd be better designed as a layer around Next and activated via normal cache headers. Continuing down the current route as it stands kinda concerns me for reasons that Ivan points out, as well as a general concern for the coherence of Next itself.

Next.js already sets the correct caching headers so that it can be cached on a CDN as well automatically when using `revalidate`. The built-in store is there for cases where people do not use a CDN but still want to leverage the revalidate behavior.

The behavior between revalidate with `getStaticProps` is quite a bit different than "just set a caching header". For example what you're pointing out is not thinking about the initial response that could have been pre-rendered at build time instead of at runtime, which can be done in a lot of cases. We've already seen this approach work out well for numerous sites.

Furthermore most CDN providers do not do global purging, e.g. picking up a static file from another edge where it was generated already, so the approach that you're outlining would cause a slowed (latency + data fetching + rendering) response for every single CDN edge the CDN provider has instead of a cached response from Next.js that is only slowed down by latency. The Vercel edge network does global purging btw so that's not a concern when hosting on Vercel, we're going to publish a blogpost on that soon (global purging).

> Continuing down the current route as it stands kinda concerns me for reasons that Ivan points out, as well as a general concern for the coherence of Next itself

Do note you can just keep using `getServerSideProps` with caching headers if you do not like the trade-off of `getStaticProps` revalidation.

author: ivawzh
text:
@lukebarton I share exactly the same feelings. I have spent a long time figuring out what the differences are between getStaticProps VS GSSP, and what they imply to CDN flows. The differences are minor but noticeable.

From my understanding, getStaticProps + fallback + regen = getServerSideProps but with extra benefits:

1. Pre-rendered at initial buildtime. I.e. no SSR on first hits by CDN.
1. Application layer `stale-while-revalidate`. I.e. no sync SSR on hits by CDN after cache expiry.

There are also obvious downsides from `fallback + regen`, such as 

1. Making server stateful. This is the root cause of my original question.
1. Buildtime complexity. 
    1. Prerendering requires extra runtime accesses during `build`, e.g. prod db connection, API connection, private subnet access, db migration, etc. 
    1. Redeployment and rollback will be tricky. As old deployment will come with outdated static props. And these static props won't expire until revalidation timeout.

From the roadmap, I can see NextJS is doubling down the static-prop-regen path. I don't have any issues against it. Just hope the side-effects and mitigations can be better thought through and documented somewhere.

Re my own `Buildtime complexity`, I think NextJS can offer an option to prerender at runtime - static props are only generated after `next start`. So that, (1) it doesn't require db or private subnet access at buildtime. (2) the generated static props won't be outdated during redeployment.

author: lukebarton
text:
> The behavior between revalidate with `getStaticProps` is quite a bit different than "just set a caching header". For example what you're pointing out is not thinking about the initial response that could have been pre-rendered at build time instead of at runtime, which can be done in a lot of cases.

Sure. But i's not really any different to calling `getServerSideProps` at build time, and pre-populating the application cache. `getStaticProps` is just a `getServerSideProps` that's run at build time, that pre-populates the built-in store that eventually gets served. 

The point I'm making is that you could use `getServerSideProps` and continue to use `getStaticPaths` but call `getServerSideProps` at build time instead of `getStaticProps`, and you could then use your built-in store to cache the result based on the cache headers that are provided on the `res` rather than Next-specific configuration properties like `revalidate: number`. Currently, it looks like Next is gaining caching-proxy like functionality through extra methods like `getStaticProps` and `revalidate: number` properties - this could be done by introducing a caching layer at the application-edge.

I doubt you use express under the hood, but imagine for a moment an express middleware that intercepts requests and serves from it's cache if it gets a hit, or goes through to the real handler and then caches the result based on the `cache-control` headers. This would give you your cache for people who don't have a CDN and lets users control it just using standard `cache-control` headers, through a simplified `getStaticPaths`+`getServerSideProps`-only interface, which you could run at build-time to pre-generate your static content that you then use to pre-seed the store that the cache uses. To me that seems preferable to replicating little bits of what a caching proxy would do by building bespoke framework APIs instead of existing `cache-control` header directives. Another use case that this would satisfy is, let's say you had a page that expired at a specific time,  for example at 2020-08-01 13:00:00. If the architecture was as I described, this resource could be statically generated _and_ naturally expire, perhaps even before the application even gets deployed. So now you can "Statically Generate pages that have an absolute expiry time" too, all for free, because you're not relying on Next re-implementing a bunch of caching behaviour with it's own unique API in the form of `getStaticProps` etc.

Sorry for the challenge, it's my contribution. Hopefully it's enlightening. Maybe there's a very good reason `cache-control` headers aren't good enough, necessitating `getStaticProps` and I just don't know what it is. But `cache-control` headers seem like a great way to indicate the validity period of content, externally and internally.

author: Timer
text:
You seem to have the correct understanding with this asterisk: 

> But you would also hit revalidate timeout sooner – which could be a smaller issue than I originally thought it would be.

Hitting your revalidate timeout "soon" isn't a bad thing. Users won't ever miss something due to it "expiring."

This would only become problematic if your CMS provider charged _per request_, but it'd still be bounded to 1 request per second, per actively visited path.

A common pattern we see is setting `revalidate: 1` and then requesting the page **only after** a CMS update is made (via a webhook). This results in much fewer CMS API requests, unless if you're having a real visitor every second.

---

FWIW we are working on an on-demand invalidation API that we're hoping to post a RFC for in the next couple months.

Ugh. I am now currently dealing with this issue. On a box running 24+ nextjs processes, the nodes desyncing from each other made a 5 minute revalidation appear to be a 30+ minute revalidate unless we repeatedly spammed the page, all the while sending different versions of the page upon different refreshes.

Question though, since it's clearly an application level cache, are the caches committed to disk? If they are, why isn't it using the `stat.mtime` to determine freshness instead of having an in memory manifest? Sure disks are slower than memory, but if its a fs based cache, not only do you get immediate sync between node processes, but you can also make it a multi-machine sync using an nfs mount (if you find small padded white rooms with psychologists running around your gig). Further, it write locks so you can prevent other nodes from regenerating (continue serving stale) while the responsible node handling the revalidate does its thing.

You could make it so the manifest is written to disk when changed and have the nextjs process watch and reload manifest when that happens. This implies that the revalidated files are already committed to disk before manifest is written, but it would be a quick and dirty multi-process manifest sync.

If the cache isnt written to disk, why not? For small sites, sure, SSG in memory seems fine, but if you have it hooked to a headless cms and a prolific content team, that's asking for memory issues, right? Maybe keep the current manifest memory strategy as an option, but provide another file system strategy, or even a redis strategy would make SSG extremely powerful.

Unfortunately, judging from this discussion, I am going to have to disable `revalidate`, possibly SSG entirely, and push stale-while-revalidate off to a cdn to manage instead. It's a great feature running a single process, but it's hopelessly broken for multiprocess deployments as it currently stands.

author: javiercr
text:
The problem with SEO is that it's a very obscure topic and Google often doesn't provide enough clarity, so we all tend to play along with the few things we do know for sure.

What we know for sure is that serving Googlebot with content-rich HTML as fast as possible works (and that's why people like Static Site Generation).

However, IMHO serving content-rich HTML (thanks to blocking SSR) to Googlebot, and a skeleton (+ client side data fetching and rendering) to users, falls under the dated but official definitions of cloaking.

How does Google checks for cloaking? That's a mystery, therefore it's hard to tell whether they would notice the difference. If they did test this by fetching as Googlebot with JS disabled and then as "user" (no Googlebot user-agent) with JS enabled, the final result (after client side rendering) would be the same, and they wouldn't be able to tell the difference. However if they tested the user experience just by changing the user-agent but without enabling JS, they would see just the skeleton, and they may think the Googlebot version is cloaked to make the site look like if it had content that doesn't have.

Don't take me wrong, I do think the "smart mode" makes a lot of sense, and it's the best experience possible for everyone, but we need to be confident Google is ok with that too. Any further details would be more than appreciated!

author: lukebarton
text:
`getStaticProps` w/ Next's cache is not really far removed from `getServerSideProps` w/ your own cache. The difference is whether you render at build time, or runtime. The fact you can `fallback: true` and run `getStaticProps` once at runtime, is a way to deal with cache misses. Having a real cache, that's been designed to have its cache invalidated (you can invalidate keys programmatically, all caches offer this API) will save you from waiting for Next.js to implement their own cache invalidation. Running Next.js's `getStaticProps` with `revalidate` or `fallback` with redundancy in a cluster is no fun either.

But yes, you should be trying to fetch time-sensitive things on the client. For your less-time-sensitive serverside rendered response,  if you need to periodically update the things you've pre-rendered, I'd definitely just render at runtime and bring your own cache, rather than trying to jump through all of the obstacles that `getStaticProps` introduces, and features it lacks. If you can deploy your pre-rendered content and forget about it, then `getStaticProps` is fine. It's equivalent to pre-populating a cache, but it's a home-rolled Next.js one that you're going to have to wait for them to develop solutions for cache invalidation.

author: xiata
text:
If you are only running one process on a single server, ignore this reply (though heed the warning if you try to go multi-process or multi-server):

With the current implementation, if you ever plan on having high availability, either on the same machine or spread across multiple servers, I honestly highly recommend you avoid this feature all together and instead rely on some other tooling to perform the caching for you. It comes down to these reasons:

- ISG does not notify other running next.js processes of updates. This means that if node#1 updates during revalidation, node#2 is completely unaware of it, and if you have load balancing between `node#1...node#n`, it will require at least `2n` requests to see the new content consistently between nodes (each node first serving a stale response before sending the updated version). This is only if a perfectly round-robin approach is used, it can degenerate into inconsistent responses for a significant period of time if a non-deterministic approach is used.
- ISG when used with hidden option `experimental.sprFlushToDisk` does not notify other processes actively (signal other processes) or passively (each process fs.watchFile on the manifest to reload it). Technically if you have a script watch and have `pm2 gracefulReload`, it could probably achieve this, however, this likely will lead to failures so don't.
- It was mentioned above about potentially using a proxy (varnish, nginx, etc) in front of next.js as a caching layer. It's a good idea, but again-- **don't use it with ISG**. If something else is handling caching for you, you don't want to have it serve from a cache incoherent backend because it will cache stale versions like mentioned in the `node#1...node#n` manner (serving different versions for a much longer time due to the cache being invalid). Luckily, we already have `getServerSideProps`, which works well with a cache layer in front of it.

Personally, I believe varnish would be the best proxying/caching tool for you for use in conjunction with next.js, specifically if when your products change price, you can issue PURGE requests to drop the cache for known URLs: https://varnish-cache.org/docs/trunk/users-guide/purging.html
A wildcard purge example: https://gist.github.com/ismasan/798947

author: lukebarton
text:
The OP comment sounds like a bug with Vercel's hosting platform rather than Next.js.

https://vercel.com/docs/edge-network/caching#x-vercel-cache

`HIT` should indicate that the response was served from the edge. I'd expect this would NOT also fetch from the upstream (ie. your Next.js app), which is also what the OP comment appears to expect too.

Vercel's `x-vercel-cache` is a Vercel thing rather than a Next.js thing. I'd raise a support issue with Vercel @pueyo5 

### Re: people with revalidate caching issues

The best solution is to not even hit your application. Let a CDN serve a response that's been cached, rather than your application. Trying to share disks/Redis's to sync up application caches is the wrong path - sure you _could_ do it but it's a bunch of unnecessary complexity. Moving your caching solution in front of your application is a far better design.

Using [Vercel](https://vercel.com/pricing) should (caveat: this bug) take care of all of this for you. That's what Vercel want from Next.js - for you to use Vercel hosting, Vercel is a for-profit company after all. "It's all about that developer experience".

If you're running this on your own, I suggest not running multiple instances and trying to share disk caches. By all means, use multiple instances ("High Availability") but put a cache in front of your application (AWS CloudFront <super easy>, CloudFlare, Akamai etc) instead of using the runtime application cache _inside_ Next.js.

A response header like `cache-control: max-age=60` will tell the CDN to cache it for 60 seconds before ever asking the application server for it again.
In comparison `revalidate: 60` will make Next.js write the response to disk and keep serving it for 60 seconds. Without the CDN, your application will be hit with every request, but it'll be served from disk. This is per instance of your Next.js application, which matters if you're loadbalancing, HA, or even serverless, each function call being a new instance. This is why you might be looking to share disks and Redis instances. That's the complicated solution. The CDN approach is a simpler design, cheaper, and definitely less hassle.

author: cbdeveloper
text:
I'm using `revalidate` on my blogging website, but I've run into a huge caveat. The problem is that  `next/link` client-side transitions do not trigger the revalidation. They always get the pre-built / pre-fetched json props. They never trigger the `getStaticProps` again. Even worse, the prefetched json is cached on client, so even if you transition to a page that has been revalidated by some other request, you still get stale client-cached pre-fetched data. A user might get stuck on a stale version of your website page for ever.

Can we have a way to trigger page revalidation with client-side transitions using `next/link` ?

I had to update my whole website to use regular `<a>` tags instead of client-side transitions, to make sure pages will be revalidated.

Anyone else facing this?

author: lucasconstantino
text:
**About cache-tags/surrogate-keys**
Regenerating based on URLs is limited, as it can be very tricky to understand what exact pages should be revalidated upon some data change. [Fastly](https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/working-with-surrogate-keys#:~:text=Surrogate%20keys%20are%20unique%20identifiers,to%20selectively%20purge%20related%20content.) (and [Varnish](https://varnish-cache.org/)) provide a way to _tag_ cache items – in our case, rendered pages – with identifiers that inform what datawas used to generate a specific page. With that, it becomes way easier to revalidate any page in the system upon changes to that data or group of data.

I just released a package to perform revalidation of Next.js ISR pages using this solution: [next-cache-tags](https://github.com/lucasconstantino/next-cache-tags).

I hope it brings further discussions on ways that Next.js could better integrate such concept into core.
